tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).
- Subagents run in the background by default; you'll be notified when one completes. Pass `run_in_background: false` only when your very next action depends on the result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise background it so the user can interject. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.

1	# kitty — shared trip expenses: design
2	
3	## Intent
4	
5	Friends on group trips currently settle up with spreadsheets and arguments at
6	the end. `kitty` replaces that with something **simple and predictable**: a
7	command-line tool that records who paid what, how each cost is split, and at
8	the end says who owes whom. Every number it prints must be reproducible by
9	hand from the rules below — no hidden rounding, no surprising re-computation.
10	
11	## Goals
12	
13	- Record members, expenses (with flexible splits and currencies) and repayments.
14	- Show balances, a deterministic settle-up plan, per-person history, a
15	  per-category spending report, and a CSV export.
16	- Scriptable: reporting commands print JSON in fixed shapes.
17	- Robust: bad input is a clean error, never a traceback, never a corrupted file.
18	
19	## Non-goals
20	
21	- Fewest-possible-payments optimisation (settle uses a specific greedy method).
22	- Live exchange rates, multiple kitties per folder, editing entries in place
23	  (remove and re-add instead), listing/removing payments (not requested; can
24	  be added later), any third-party dependency.
25	
26	## Anti-goals (would be a failure even if it "works")
27	
28	- Balances that don't sum to exactly zero, or that change on their own
29	  (e.g. because a rate was changed later).
30	- Floating-point arithmetic anywhere in money handling.
31	- An error that leaves `kitty.json` partially written or modified.
32	
33	## Constraints
34	
35	- Python standard library only. Must run on **Python 3.9** (the installed
36	  version is 3.9.6) — no `match`, no `X | Y` type syntax at runtime.
37	- Run as `python3 -m kitty <command>` from the project folder (package `kitty/`
38	  with `__main__.py`).
39	- All state in `kitty.json` in the current working directory.
40	
41	## Approaches considered
42	
43	1. **Small package with separated layers (chosen).** `money.py` (parsing,
44	   conversion, cent-splitting — pure functions on int cents / `Decimal`),
45	   `ledger.py` (members, expenses, payments, balances, settle, history,
46	   report — pure logic over loaded data), `storage.py` (read/write
47	   `kitty.json`), `cli.py` (argparse, JSON output, error → exit 1). Tests with
48	   `unittest`, both unit-level on the money rules and end-to-end through the
49	   real command in a temp directory. Chosen because the rounding rules are what
50	   the user most needs to trust, so they must be isolated and directly tested.
51	2. **Event log, recompute everything on each run.** Little benefit because
52	   rates and splits are locked at record time; adds a way for results to drift.
53	3. **Single-file script.** Faster to write, but mixes money logic with CLI
54	   parsing and fights the `python3 -m kitty` package layout.
55	
56	## Data rules (decided by the user)
57	
58	### Money and amounts
59	- All arithmetic uses `Decimal` / integer cents. Never floats.
60	- An amount argument must be a positive number with at most two decimal
61	  places. `12.345`, `0`, `-5`, `abc` are errors (no rounding of input).
62	- Output money is a string with exactly two decimals, e.g. `"41.40"`,
63	  `"-20.70"`.
64	
65	### Currencies and rates
66	- Currency codes are three letters, accepted in any case, stored uppercase.
67	- `init EUR` sets the base currency. The base currency always has rate 1.
68	- `rate set USD 0.92` means 1 USD = 0.92 base. Setting a rate for the base
69	  currency is an error. Rate must be a positive decimal.
70	- Conversion: `amount × rate`, rounded to the cent, **halves rounded up**
71	  (`ROUND_HALF_UP`).
72	- Each expense and payment **stores the rate in force when it was added** and
73	  its converted base amount. Later `rate set` never changes existing entries.
74	- Using a currency with no rate set is an error.
75	
76	### Splitting (always in base-currency cents, after conversion)
77	Let `T` be the converted base total in cents.
78	- **Equal (default: everyone)**: participants are all current members in the
79	  order they joined. Each gets `floor(T / n)`; the leftover cents go one each
80	  to participants in order. 10.00 among Alice, Bob, Cara → 3.34, 3.33, 3.33.
81	- **`--among A,B`**: same as equal, among only those listed, in the order
82	  listed.
83	- **`--shares A=2,B=1`**: weights are positive whole numbers. Each portion is
84	  `floor(T × w / Σw)`; leftover cents go one each in listed order.
85	  10.00 with `A=1,B=2` → A 3.34, B 6.66.
86	- **`--percent A=60,B=40`**: values must total exactly 100; handled as
87	  weights exactly like shares (portion `floor(T × p / 100)`, leftovers in
88	  listed order).
89	- **`--exact A=30,B=20`**: values are in the expense's own currency and must
90	  add up exactly to the expense amount (else error); then they are treated as
91	  weights on `T` exactly like shares.
92	- Only one of `--among`, `--exact`, `--shares`, `--percent` per expense.
93	- Every name in a split must be a current member; no name may appear twice.
94	- Splits are computed **once, when the expense is added**, and stored. Members
95	  who join later are not part of earlier "everyone" expenses.
96	- Shares therefore always sum to exactly `T`.
97	
98	### Members
99	- Names are **case-insensitive**: "alice" and "Alice" are the same person.
100	  Adding a name that matches an existing one case-insensitively is an error.
101	  Every command accepts any spelling; output always uses the name as first
102	  added.
103	- Names may not contain `,` or `=`. (Builder's call: also reject empty /
104	  whitespace-only names.)
105	- Join order is preserved and matters (equal splits, output order).
106	- `member remove` is refused if the person appears anywhere: as payer or
107	  sharer of any expense, or sender/recipient of any payment. Removing someone
108	  with no history is fine.
109	
110	### Payments
111	- `payment add FROM TO AMOUNT [--currency C] [--date D]`: FROM's balance goes
112	  up by the base amount, TO's goes down. FROM and TO the same person is an
113	  error. Both must be members.
114	
115	### Balances
116	- For each member: `Σ(base amounts they paid) − Σ(their shares) +
117	  Σ(payments sent) − Σ(payments received)`. Positive = owed money.
118	
119	### Settle (greedy, deterministic)
120	While anyone has a nonzero balance: the person who owes the most (most
121	negative) pays the person who is owed the most (most positive) the smaller of
122	the two absolute amounts, so at least one of them reaches zero. Ties on either
123	side go to the name that comes first alphabetically, ignoring case
124	(`str.casefold`). Payments are listed in the order they are worked out.
125	`settle` only suggests; it records nothing.
126	
127	### Dates and categories
128	- `--date YYYY-MM-DD`, validated as a real date; default is today.
129	- `--category`, default `"other"`.
130	
131	### IDs
132	- Expenses are numbered 1, 2, 3, … ; an ID is never reused, even after
133	  removal (store a `next_id` counter).
134	
135	## Commands and output
136	
137	Reporting commands print JSON via `json.dumps` with default separators (which
138	matches the examples below exactly), followed by a newline.
139	
140	| Command | Output |
141	|---|---|
142	| `init CUR` | nothing |
143	| `member add NAME` / `member remove NAME` | nothing |
144	| `member list` | `["Alice", "Bob"]` (join order) |
145	| `expense add PAYER AMOUNT DESCRIPTION [opts]` | the new ID alone, e.g. `1` |
146	| `expense list` | see below (ID order) |
147	| `expense remove ID` | nothing; unknown ID is an error |
148	| `payment add FROM TO AMOUNT [--currency] [--date]` | nothing |
149	| `rate set CUR RATE` | nothing |
150	| `balances` | `{"Alice": "20.70", "Bob": "-20.70"}` |
151	| `settle` | `[{"from": "Bob", "to": "Alice", "amount": "20.70"}]` |
152	| `history NAME` | `[{"date": ..., "description": ..., "change": ..., "balance": ...}]` |
153	| `report` | `{"food": {"Alice": "20.70", "Bob": "20.70"}}` |
154	| `export FILE` | nothing; writes CSV |
155	
156	`expense list` entry:
157	`{"id": 1, "date": "2026-07-14", "payer": "Alice", "description": "Dinner",

tools.name: Agent
tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).
- Subagents run in the background by default; you'll be notified when one completes. Pass `run_in_background: false` only when your very next action depends on the result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise background it so the user can interject. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.
